issues.explanation: The trigger 'Arab villages' is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of physical abuse by a romantic partner and the rest of the profile, which centers on interpersonal abuse-related cues, self-appraisals, and memory phenomena. Without any corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal content involving war, military, or ethnic/geographic conflict, this item appears clinically incoherent for this patient.

issues.item: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Strictly restricting eating to feel in control is not well supported by the rest of the profile. The other selected items coherently describe PTSD related to partner physical abuse (criticism, violence, offender cues; fragmented/alien memory; rage; dehumanization, self-blame, emotional numbing; distraction and cue avoidance). In contrast, restrictive eating introduces a distinct control-focused coping pattern that is not reflected elsewhere in triggers, memory, threat, or appraisals, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same formulation rather than a separate problem.

vignette: Hemi was sixty-two when the relationship he had trusted for nearly two decades ended in a sudden eruption of violence in their Seattle kitchen. He had been folding laundry when his partner, overwhelmed by stress, suddenly hurled a heavy iron skillet across the room, striking his shoulder before grabbing his wrist and pinning him against the cabinets. The sharp crack of metal on wood, the smell of spilled coffee, and his partner’s narrowed eyes remain lodged in his mind not as a flowing sequence of events, but as a few frozen, picture-like moments that replay whenever the air grows tense. Whenever the sharp clack of heavy objects or the sight of a man with similar broad shoulders crossed his path, these specific cues would instantly pull his mind back to those frozen pictures, cementing the visual fragments as his primary reality. Hemi tells himself now that he is wired to attract such brutality, a conviction that took hold immediately after he packed his bags. This deep-seated belief that he was fundamentally flawed shaped how he processed the trauma; because he had come to view himself as inherently defective, the memory of the assault never softened into a coherent narrative, instead hardening into a series of jagged, alien snapshots that felt like they belonged to a stranger rather than to him. Over the following months, Hemi’s daily routine as a senior manuscript editor became a minefield of carefully calculated escapes. The sudden return of those picture-like memories would inevitably spill across his oak desk, compelling him to immediately abandon his proofs and scroll through unrelated news articles until his breathing steadied. This reflexive diversion of focus became his primary defense, but it only succeeded in keeping his emotional life locked in a rigid, unprocessed state, preventing any natural resolution. The heavy manuscripts now felt like extensions of his former partner’s grip, their red-inked margins looking like bruises against the white pages. He began requesting remote work, isolating himself in his home office where the only sounds were the quiet tap of his keyboard and the distant hum of traffic. This isolation only succeeded in keeping his feelings at a distance, reinforcing his conviction that he was permanently stripped of normal emotion and fundamentally broken. The very habit of diverting his attention whenever he felt vulnerable cemented this self-judgment, which in turn made him hypersensitive to the slightest hint of correction from his colleagues. When a junior copywriter sent him an email questioning a passage, the sudden wave of criticism instantly triggered a familiar tightness in his chest, pushing him back toward the same mental escape routes. The loop tightened with each passing year, as the fractured, alien memories of the assault would occasionally surface during his commute, instantly flooding him with a fresh wave of rage that made him grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened. That sudden flare of fury did not fade quietly; it pulled his attention back to the parking lot of the publishing house, where he would deliberately take a longer route to avoid passing the building where his former partner once worked, ensuring that seeing anyone who resembled the abuser was completely out of reach. Every time he successfully avoided the sight of a similar-looking man or shut down the anger before it could spread, the avoidance only validated his fear that his own nature was irreparably damaged. Consequently, when a new editor at his firm gently suggested he reconsider a recurring phrasing error in his proofs, Hemi found himself abruptly leaving the office early, the phantom weight of a previous blow dictating his retreat. Now, at seventy-four, divorced and living alone, Hemi finally sought therapy after a recent promotion review triggered a dissociative episode where he felt entirely like an object in his own workspace. He is terrified that the therapist will see the defectiveness he has spent decades hiding, yet he desperately hopes someone might finally help him untangle the frozen memories before the numbness takes everything else.
